name: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
title: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
answer: Board advisory and fiduciary risk covers the duties directors owe when artificial intelligence enters the decisions, products or operations of a company. It sits inside corporate governance and regulatory compliance, and it reaches the boardroom rather than the engineering team. The subject includes oversight of AI use, disclosure to investors, and the question of what a director must ask before approving an AI programme. It also covers the exposure that follows when those duties are tested in court.

sections.body: Board advisory and fiduciary risk covers the duties directors owe when artificial intelligence enters the decisions, products or operations of a company. It sits inside corporate governance and regulatory compliance, and it reaches the boardroom rather than the engineering team. The subject includes oversight of AI use, disclosure to investors, and the question of what a director must ask before approving an AI programme. It also covers the exposure that follows when those duties are tested in court.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the ordinary machinery of governance: board and committee papers, minutes, charters, delegation schedules, and management reporting lines. AI specific material is layered on top, such as model inventories, risk registers, vendor contracts, audit findings and incident logs. Directors rarely touch the models themselves, so the practical infrastructure is the reporting chain that carries AI risk upward in a form a board can act on. Registers of applicable rules and litigation trackers feed the same pipeline.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Advisers begin by mapping where AI touches the business and which existing duties already apply, then translate technical facts into board level language. They build oversight structures, set reporting cadence, and draft questions directors can put to management. Diligence on vendors, data and model provenance is folded into the same review. Where disputes arise, the analysis turns on what the board knew, when it knew it, and what it did next, which is why minutes and escalation records carry so much weight.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Fiduciary duty, disclosure obligations and the business judgment rule frame most of the analysis, alongside sector regulators and state legislation. The site tracks 150 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which together show how quickly the questions are moving from theory into pleadings. Provenance matters on both sides: where training data came from, and where a board's own record of oversight came from. Directors also face personal exposure in some jurisdictions, so indemnification, insurance and conflicts policies sit inside the same picture.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more litigation testing what oversight actually requires, and more state bills setting disclosure and accountability duties, against the 7166 already tracked here. Boards are likely to formalise AI committees or fold the topic into existing risk committees, with standing reporting rather than one off briefings. Regulation and case law will keep shifting the baseline, so the practical direction is toward documented, repeatable oversight that can be shown after the fact. The open question is how far courts will hold directors responsible for technical failures they cannot personally evaluate.
